Acknowledgments

The Dominican Republic Country Economic Memorandum (CEM) was prepared with the leadership and support of the Country Management Unit (CMU) led by Michel Kerf (Country Director, LCC2C) and Alexandria Valerio (Resident Representative, LCCDO). The team benefited from technical support and guidance from Doerte Doemeland (Practice Manager, ELCMU) and Pedro L. Rodriguez (Lead Country Economist, ELCDR).

Constructive feedback and discussions were received from counterparts from the Ministry of Economy, Planning and Development (MEPyD), led by Mr. Pavel Isa (Minister), and included: Miguel Ceara (former minister), Alexis Cruz-Rodriguez (Vice Minister of Economic and Social Analysis), Evalina Gomez (Director of Sectoral Economic Analysis) and Rosa Cañete (Director of Poverty, Inequality and Democratic Culture); likewise, the National Competitiveness Council (CNC) significantly contributed in the development of the narrative, with comments provided by the CNC president, Peter A. Prazmowski, and Katherine Javier (Director of the Competitiveness Intelligence unit); in addition, relevant suggestions were provided by the Analysis and Fiscal Policy unit from the Ministry of Finance, led by Camila Hernandez, the Economic and Taxes Study unit led by Patricia Gil, as well as other members of the Ministry of Finance. The National Statistical Office (ONE) as coordinated by Augusto de los Santos, played an important role by providing relevant information for several chapters of the report. The CEM benefited from consultations from private sector organizations, and academia, specifically Raul Hernandez, director of the national pension association and advisor of private sector companies, provided insightful comments for Chapter 2.

The task team was led by James Sampi (Economist, ELCMU) and Johannes Herderschee (until April 2022, Senior Economist, CELCE). Gabriel Zaourak (Senior Economist, ELCMU) finalized the report. The team consisted of Sebastian Galiani (Professor, University of Maryland), Jorge Thompson Araujo (Senior Research Fellow, University of Brasilia and Consultant ELCMU), Paola Brens (Consultant, ELCMU), Milagros Deza (Consultant, ELCMU) and Ivana Benzaquen (Consultant, ELCMU), who provided inputs for the macroeconomic analysis in the Chapter 1, while the regional GDP estimates was led by Jose Pablo Valdez (Senior Economist, DECES) and Charl Jooste (Senior Economist, EMFMD) provided advice on the macro structural forecasts; Dong Dao (Consultant, ELCMU), and Alexis Cruz (MEPyD) contributed in the productivity analysis of Chapter 2; while Hasan Dudu (Senior Economist, EMFMD), Martin Christensen (Economist, EMFMD) and Carmen Estrades (Consultant, ELCMU) led the model simulations, with contributions from Huong Nguyen (Energy Specialist, ILCE1) for the energy scenario. The competition policy analysis in chapter 3 was led by Denis Sanchez (Economist, ETIMT), with contributions from Seidu Dauda (Economist, ETIMT) and Soulange Gramegna (Consultant, ETIMT), under the guidance of Martha Licetti (Practice Manager, ETIMT) and Graciela Miralles (Senior Economist, ETIMT), while Maria Scheker (Procurement Specialist, ELCRU), Paola Brens (Consultant, ELCMU) and Milagros Deza (Consultant, ELCMU) contributed for the procurement analysis of Chapter 4.

Anjali Shahani (Operations Officer, ELCMU), Giselle Velasquez (Program Assistant, ELCMU), Benjamin Vuilleminroy (Program Assistant, ELCMU), and Maria J. Hermann (Executive Assistant, LCCDO) provided valuable administrative and logistical support.

The team thanks the CEM peer reviewers for their helpful suggestions and insights: Marc Schiffbauer (Senior Economist, EECM2), Ana Cusolito (Senior Economist, ETIMT), Guillermo Vuletin (Senior Economist, LCRCE), Daniel Riera-Crichton (Senior Economist, LCRCE), Samuel Pienknagura (Senior Economist, IMF) and Fausto Patino (Economist, ELCFN).

Abstract The Dominican Republic’s growth model has led to exceptional economic expansion, far exceeding the LAC average over the past two decades, but it is reaching its limits due to slow productivity growth. While impressive, the Dominican Republic’s growth performance has been based on factor accumulation rather than productivity growth and associated with regional disparities and wage stagnation. Productivity growth has been hindered by policy distortions, climate-related natural disasters as well as inadequate human capital. A new round of structural reforms will boost productivity growth, including by: (i) unleashing its human capital potential; (ii) fomenting competitive markets; (iii) revamping the innovation strategy; (iv) reducing public expenditure inefficiencies; and (v) strengthening resilience against external shocks and climate change.

Executive summary

The Dominican Republic’s growth model has led to exceptional economic expansion, but it is reaching its limits due to slow productivity growth

The Dominican Republic’s macroeconomic performance exceeded the regional Latin America and the Caribben (LAC) average over the past two decades, leading to a rapid convergence towards the US in per capita levels. The Dominican Republic pursued economic reforms between the 1990s and early 2000s—including the liberalization of foreign exchange transactions and trade, and elimination of price controls and restrictions to foreign direct investment (FDI). These reforms accelerated economic growth in the following decades, which averaged 5.8 during the 2005-2019 period. Favorable geographical and external economic conditions also boosted growth, as did a combination of economic incentives that attracted investment.

However, the Dominican Republic’s recent growth model has been based on factor accumulation rather than productivity growth. Capital formation has been the main contributor of economic growth, accounting for 3.7 percentage points of GDP growth on average between 2005 and 2019. Employment was responsible for a non-negligible 1.6 percentage-point rise in GDP over the same period, with labor quality only contributing 0.4 percentage points. After the banking crisis of 2003/2004, Total Factor Productivity’s (TFP) contribution to GDP growth has been positive—unlike that in most of LAC countries. However, it has not increased in lockstep with per capita income. Productivity in the Dominican Republic caught up with the U.S. by the mid-1990s. However, due to the absence of further reforms, it receded back to 60 percent by 2019, well below both structural and aspirational peer economies such as Costa Rica and Uruguay, respectively.

The Dominican Republic’s growth model has also been associated with wage stagnation and regional disparities

Lagging productivity contributed to depressed real wages in a country with already high regional disparities. Although GDP per capita in the country is among the highest in the LAC region, average monthly earnings are among the lowest— the average wage in countries with a similar income level, such as Costa Rica, is nearly three times higher (Figure i). Despite rapid economic growth, the share of the population that is considered vulnerable (i.e., with an income between US$5.50 and US$13 per day in PPP) increased from 38.1 percent in 2005 to 43.7 percent in 2019. 1 Similarly, depressed real wages contributed to consumption welfare inequality with growth benefits accruing only to a handful of regions. The richest 1 percent of households accounts for nearly 10 percent of national income – nearly 4 percentage points higher compared to countries such as Uruguay. Furthermore, income gaps by gender are sizable. Income per capita in the regions of Ozama or Yuma is significantly higher than in poorer regions such as Enriquillo or El Valle. Figure i. Faster productivity would fuel economic growth in the medium and long run, especially for the poorest households. A one percentage point increase in TFP above its historical average would lift GDP growth to nearly 7 percent, enabling a rapid convergence with the living standards of high-income countries. Productivity enhancing reforms would increase the average income of the poorest households by nearly 17 percent by 2030, and almost double the income by 2050.

Productivity growth has been hindered by policy distortions, climate-related natural disasters and inadequate human capital
